nodes.title: Foundations and Core Language
nodes.description: This part groups chapters in this subject’s graduate book.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Homotopy and fundamental groups
nodes.description: Homotopy compares maps through continuous deformation. The fundamental group records based loops modulo based homotopy.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Homotopies
nodes.description: Homotopy compares maps through continuous deformation. It provides a flexible equivalence notion that preserves many algebraic invariants.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Homotopy equivalence
nodes.description: A homotopy equivalence is a map with an inverse up to homotopy. It identifies spaces with the same homotopy-level structure.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Deformation retracts
nodes.description: A deformation retract continuously shrinks a space onto a subspace while fixing that subspace. It gives a particularly concrete homotopy equivalence.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Homotopy invariance
nodes.description: Homotopy invariance means that homotopic maps induce the same invariant map, with the relevant basepoint conventions. This allows continuous deformations to simplify computations.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Fundamental group
nodes.description: The fundamental group records based loops modulo based homotopy. It detects obstructions to contracting loops and supports covering-space theory.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Loops and basepoints
nodes.description: A based loop begins and ends at a specified point. Concatenation and reversal define the fundamental group operation and inverse.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Van Kampen theorem
nodes.description: Van Kampen computes a fundamental group from compatible open pieces under its connectivity hypotheses. It describes how generators and relations assemble across overlaps.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Computations
nodes.description: Circles, bouquets, and surfaces provide standard fundamental-group computations. These examples establish how geometric identifications produce algebraic relations.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Covering spaces
nodes.description: Covering maps locally present a space as disjoint copies of the base. Deck transformations are automorphisms of a covering over its base.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Covering maps
nodes.description: Covering maps locally present a space as disjoint copies of the base. Lifting properties translate topology into discrete and group-theoretic data.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Lifting properties
nodes.description: Lifting asks whether a map into the base can be realized upstairs in the covering space. Existence and uniqueness depend on the map, basepoint, and covering hypotheses.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Path and homotopy lifting
nodes.description: Paths lift uniquely after choosing a starting point, and suitable homotopies lift compatibly. These facts connect covering spaces to the fundamental group.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Classification hypotheses
nodes.description: The standard subgroup classification assumes a connected, locally path-connected, semilocally simply connected base. Without these assumptions, familiar conclusions can fail.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Deck transformations
nodes.description: Deck transformations are automorphisms of a covering over its base. Universal covers make their relation to fundamental groups especially clear.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Universal covers
nodes.description: A universal cover is a simply connected covering space when it exists. It supplies a common source for connected coverings in the standard setting.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Group actions
nodes.description: Appropriate properly discontinuous group actions produce covering quotients. Deck groups record the corresponding symmetries upstairs.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Examples from surfaces
nodes.description: The plane covering a torus and related surface examples make lifting visible. Their deck transformations connect geometry with familiar groups.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Singular homology
nodes.description: Singular homology turns maps from simplices into algebraic chain complexes. Homology assigns algebraic maps to continuous maps.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Chain complexes
nodes.description: Singular homology turns maps from simplices into algebraic chain complexes. Its quotient construction measures cycles that do not bound.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Singular simplices
nodes.description: A singular simplex is a continuous map from a standard simplex into the space. Formal combinations of these maps form the chain groups.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Boundary maps
nodes.description: Boundary maps take alternating sums of face restrictions. Their successive composition is zero, making homology well defined.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Homology groups
nodes.description: A homology group is the kernel of a boundary map modulo the image of the previous one. It records cycles that survive after boundaries are identified with zero.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Functoriality and invariance
nodes.description: Homology assigns algebraic maps to continuous maps. Its invariance properties allow spaces to be replaced by simpler homotopy models.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Induced maps
nodes.description: A continuous map sends each singular simplex to its composition with that map. This defines the induced chain and homology maps.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Homotopy invariance
nodes.description: A homotopy produces a chain homotopy through a prism construction. Consequently, homotopic maps induce the same homology map.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Homology of standard spaces
nodes.description: Points, spheres, and other basic spaces calibrate the meaning of homology groups. Their calculations become inputs for more complicated decompositions.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Central Theory and Techniques
nodes.description: This part groups chapters in this subject’s graduate book.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Exact sequences and computation
nodes.description: Relative homology measures a space with a chosen subspace treated as negligible. Mayer–Vietoris computes homology from overlapping pieces.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Pairs and relative homology
nodes.description: Relative homology measures a space with a chosen subspace treated as negligible. Exact sequences and excision connect it to absolute computations.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Long exact sequence
nodes.description: The long exact sequence of a pair connects subspace, whole-space, and relative homology. Its connecting map records the boundary left inside the subspace.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Excision
nodes.description: Excision removes suitably contained parts without changing relative homology. It expresses the local nature of the relative construction.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Quotient comparison
nodes.description: For suitable pairs, relative homology agrees with reduced homology of the quotient space. The good-pair hypotheses are essential to this comparison.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Mayer–Vietoris
nodes.description: Mayer–Vietoris computes homology from overlapping pieces. It is a practical local-to-global consequence of exactness and excision.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Decomposition
nodes.description: A suitable decomposition expresses the space as pieces with a controlled overlap. Their individual homology groups become the inputs to the sequence.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Connecting maps
nodes.description: The connecting map measures the obstruction to splitting a global cycle into cycles on the pieces. Its construction explains the sequence's exactness.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Calculations
nodes.description: Sphere and surface calculations illustrate successive use of Mayer–Vietoris. Explicit maps are needed when knowing group ranks alone is insufficient.

nodes.title: CW complexes and cellular methods
nodes.description: CW complexes build spaces by attaching cells of increasing dimension. Cellular homology replaces the large singular chain complex by one generator per cell.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Cell structures
nodes.description: CW complexes build spaces by attaching cells of increasing dimension. Their skeletal organization supports efficient homotopy and homology arguments.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Attaching maps
nodes.description: An attaching map glues the boundary of a cell to the previous skeleton. It determines how that cell changes the space.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Skeleta
nodes.description: The n-skeleton contains all cells of dimension at most n. These nested subspaces form the filtration used in cellular methods.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Cellular approximation
nodes.description: Cellular approximation replaces a map between CW complexes by a homotopic cellular map under the standard theorem. It aligns maps with the skeletal structure.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Cellular homology
nodes.description: Cellular homology replaces the large singular chain complex by one generator per cell. Attaching-map degrees determine its differentials.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Boundary matrices
nodes.description: Boundary matrices record incidence coefficients between adjacent cell dimensions. Their kernels and images yield homology groups.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Degree maps
nodes.description: Degrees measure how attaching maps cover quotient spheres with orientation. These integers provide the cellular boundary coefficients.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Computations on complexes
nodes.description: Projective spaces and finite CW complexes illustrate compact computations. The examples require tracking attaching maps rather than just counting cells.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Cohomology and products
nodes.description: Cochains are algebraic functions on chains with a dual differential. Cup products give cohomology more structure than a list of groups.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Cochains
nodes.description: Cochains are algebraic functions on chains with a dual differential. Coefficients and universal coefficient theorems connect cohomology to homology.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Cochain complexes
nodes.description: A cochain complex reverses the direction of the chain differential through Hom. Its cohomology consists of cocycles modulo coboundaries.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Universal coefficient theorem
nodes.description: Universal coefficient theorems relate cohomology with specified coefficients to homology via Hom and Ext terms. They explain the effect of torsion.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Coefficients
nodes.description: Choosing integer, field, or other coefficients changes what information an invariant retains. Coefficient choices can simplify computation while losing some distinctions.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Cup products
nodes.description: Cup products give cohomology more structure than a list of groups. The resulting ring can distinguish spaces with identical additive invariants.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Graded rings
nodes.description: Cohomology with a suitable coefficient ring is a graded ring under cup product. Graded commutativity introduces signs depending on degree.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Examples
nodes.description: Tori and projective spaces illustrate different cup-product patterns. These examples show why additive groups alone do not determine cohomology rings.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Cohomological invariants
nodes.description: Products and operations in cohomology provide obstructions to maps and decompositions. Their naturality transports such information between spaces.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Higher homotopy and characteristic classes
nodes.description: Higher homotopy groups study maps from spheres in dimensions above one. Vector bundles carry linear spaces varying over a topological base.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Homotopy groups
nodes.description: Higher homotopy groups study maps from spheres in dimensions above one. Comparison theorems connect them with homology and equivalences.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Hurewicz theorem
nodes.description: Hurewicz identifies the first relevant homotopy group with homology under connectivity assumptions. It provides a route from geometric maps to computable algebra.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Whitehead theorem
nodes.description: Whitehead's theorem makes a weak homotopy equivalence between CW complexes a homotopy equivalence. The CW setting is part of the theorem's scope.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Selected computations
nodes.description: Basic sphere and product computations illustrate both the power and difficulty of higher homotopy. The chosen examples should state imported results explicitly.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Bundles and classes
nodes.description: Vector bundles carry linear spaces varying over a topological base. Characteristic classes encode obstructions and invariants of these families.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Vector bundles
nodes.description: A vector bundle is locally a product with a vector space and has linear transition maps. It generalizes the tangent bundle construction.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Euler/Chern classes
nodes.description: Euler and Chern classes assign cohomology classes to suitably oriented real or complex bundles. They detect properties such as obstructions to sections or trivializations.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Classifying spaces
nodes.description: Classifying spaces parametrize bundles through homotopy classes of maps under suitable base-space assumptions. Universal bundles turn bundle invariants into cohomological constructions.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Duality and manifolds
nodes.description: Orientations permit a manifold to carry a fundamental homology class. Poincaré duality relates cohomology and complementary-dimensional homology of manifolds.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Orientations and cap product
nodes.description: Orientations permit a manifold to carry a fundamental homology class. Cap products translate this class into duality between homology and cohomology.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Fundamental classes
nodes.description: A fundamental class encodes a consistent local orientation of a closed oriented manifold. Noncompact or boundary cases require modified formulations.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Cap product
nodes.description: The cap product combines a cohomology class with a homology class to lower dimension. Capping with the fundamental class is the map in Poincaré duality.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Intersection pairings
nodes.description: Intersection pairings measure how complementary-dimensional cycles meet. They provide a geometric interpretation of duality and cup products.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Poincaré duality
nodes.description: Poincaré duality relates cohomology and complementary-dimensional homology of manifolds. Orientation, compactness, and boundary conditions determine its exact form.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Statement and proof structure
nodes.description: For a closed oriented n-manifold, capping with the fundamental class gives the standard duality isomorphism. A proof assembles local orientation information through suitable gluing arguments.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Applications
nodes.description: Duality constrains Betti numbers, intersection forms, and possible manifold topology. It supplies checks on independent homology computations.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Manifolds with boundary
nodes.description: Manifolds with boundary require relative groups in Poincaré–Lefschetz duality. This keeps track of classes that meet the boundary.

nodes.title: Filtered complexes

nodes.title: Filtrations

nodes.title: Pages and differentials

nodes.title: Guided computations

nodes.title: Serre or cellular examples
nodes.description: Serre spectral sequences use suitable fibrations to relate base, fiber, and total-space invariants. Cellular filtrations provide another accessible source of examples.

nodes.title: Edge maps

nodes.title: Extension problems
nodes.description: An associated graded group may not determine the original group uniquely. Extension problems resolve how the surviving pieces fit together.

nodes.title: Eilenberg–Steenrod framework
nodes.description: The Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms formalize homotopy, exactness, excision, and related properties. The dimension axiom singles out ordinary homology in the classical framework.

nodes.title: Representability motivation
